Choose $d_1,\dots,d_n \in \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)$ such that $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) =  \langle d_1 \rangle \oplus \cdots \oplus \langle d_n \rangle$.
Then $d_1,\dots,d_n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}(B,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})$, so for each $j \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ we have $B_{d_j} \nsubseteq {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$
and hence we can choose $x_j \in B_{d_j} \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$.
Then $x = x_1 \cdots x_n$ is an admissible element of $B$ such that $x \notin {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$.
So (ii) holds.

Conversely, suppose that (ii) holds.
To prove (i), it suffices to show that if $i \in \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)$ and ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B)$, then $B_i \nsubseteq {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$.
So consider $i \in \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)$ and ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B)$.
By (ii), some admissible element $x$ of $B$ satisfies $x \notin {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$.
There exist nonzero homogeneous elements $x_1,\dots,x_n$ of $B$
such that $x = x_1\cdots x_n$ and $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) = \langle \deg(x_1) \rangle \oplus \cdots \oplus \langle \deg(x_n) \rangle$.
For some $j_1,\dots,j_n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$, we have $i = j_1\deg(x_1) + \cdots + j_n \deg(x_n)$, so $x_1^{j_1} \cdots x_n^{j_n} \in B_i$.
Since $x \notin {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$, we have  $x_1^{j_1} \cdots x_n^{j_n} \notin {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ and hence $B_i \nsubseteq {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$.
So (i) holds.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label {83hdtbe924239ued7owtee6}
Let $B = \bigoplus_{i \in G} B_i$ be a noetherian normal $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$-domain graded by a finite abelian group $G$.
If $B$ is saturated in codimension $1$ then $(B_0,B) \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm EXT}}$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Let $d$ be a positive integer such that $di=0$ for all $i \in G$,
and consider the subset $Y = \big\{\, x^d \, \mid \,\text{$x$ is an admissible element of $B$}\, \big\}$ of $B_0$.
Since $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Frac}}(B) / 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Frac}}(B_0)$ is an algebraic extension of fields of characteristic $0$,
we have $(	\operatorname{\text{\rm Frac}}(B_0), 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Frac}}(B)) \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm EXT}}$ by Ex.\ \ref{83uedxc5trfnbvcDFVUirybhnjYMYbgfAcfiu736}.
By Lemma \ref{d8iuyhv1i288wsx9}, $( (B_0)_y, B_y ) \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm EXT}}$ for every $y \in Y$.
By Lemma \ref{98876152r3ediwof93408eh}, no height $1$ prime ideal of $B$ contains $Y$.
So Lemma \ref{dh2763g5d4fc5a4dsErf56w7} implies that $(B_0,B) \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm EXT}}$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label {o823y48t2309fnb28}
Let $B$ be a noetherian normal $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$-domain graded by a finitely generated abelian group $G$.
\begin{enumerata}

\item If $H \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B)$ then $\big( B^{(H)} , B^{( H + \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) )} \big) \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm EXT}}$.

\item If $H \in \mathscr{X}(B)$ then $H + \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) \in \mathscr{X}(B)$.

\end{enumerata}
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
(a) Let $B = \bigoplus_{i \in G} B_i$ be the notation.
Consider the groups $X = H + \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)$ and $Y = X/H$, and  the canonical homomorphism of the quotient group $\pi : X \to Y$.
Since $H \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B)$, the group $Y = (H + \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B))/H \subseteq (H + \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B))/H \cong \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) / (H \cap \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B))$ is torsion and hence finite.
Let $A = B^{( X )}$. Since $A$ has an $X$-grading, it also has a $Y$-grading, namely
$A = \bigoplus_{ y \in Y } A_y $ where for each $y \in Y$ we define $A_y = \bigoplus_{ i \in X_y } B_i$ (with $X_y = \big\{\,i \in X\, \mid \, \pi(i) = y \, \big\}$).
{\it We always regard $A$ as being graded by the finite group $Y$.}
Since $A_0 = B^{(H)}$, it suffices to show that $(A_0,A) \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm EXT}}$.
By Lemma \ref{98767gh11dmdffkll0ahcchvr0vfesh8263543794663cnir},
$A$ is a noetherian normal $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$-domain; so, by Prop.\ \ref{83hdtbe924239ued7owtee6},
it suffices to show that $A$ is saturated in codimension~$1$.\footnote{The
$X$-graded ring $B^{( X )}$ is not necessarily saturated in codimension $1$,
but we will show that  the $Y$-graded ring $A$ is.}

Consider the inclusion $A \subseteq B$; by Lemma \ref{87654esxcvs9dfok33me4rtu5ortyo0934urud3r24}(b),
${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \mapsto {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \cap A$ is a surjective map from $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B)$ to $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(A)$.
In particular,  $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B) \neq \varnothing$ $\Leftrightarrow$ $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(A) \neq \varnothing$.
If $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(A) = \varnothing$ then (by Def.\ \ref{oi8y81726et73e8f0i349rtfyh-sat}) $A$ is saturated in codimension $1$ and we are done.
So we may assume that $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(A) \neq \varnothing$. It follows that $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B) \neq \varnothing$,
$\operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) = {\textstyle \bigcap_{ {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B)} \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}(B,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})}$ and
$\operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(A) = {\textstyle \bigcap_{ {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{q}}} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(A)} \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}(A,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{q}}}) }$.

Consider ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}(B)$. 
We claim that 
\begin{equation}  \label {87654efg172193p01d2rbtfvcxvoo39}
\pi \big( \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}(B,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \cap X \big) = \pi \big( {\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}(B,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \cap X \big) .
\end{equation}
Indeed, if $W$ is a submonoid of $X$ then $\pi(W)$ is a submonoid of the finite group $Y$, so $\pi(W)$ is a group and hence
$\pi(W) = \langle \pi(W) \rangle = \pi( \langle W \rangle )$;
so $\pi \big( {\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}(B,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \cap X \big) = \pi \big( \langle {\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}(B,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \cap X \rangle \big)$.
We have $\langle \ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}(B,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \cap X \rangle = \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}(B,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \cap X$
by Lemma \ref{jBh9823hedAcv78n2erj20} (note that $X \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B)$, because $X \supseteq H \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B)$);
so \eqref{87654efg172193p01d2rbtfvcxvoo39} follows.


For each $i \in {\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}(B,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \cap X$, we have
$B_i \nsubseteq {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$, so $A_{ \pi(i) } \nsubseteq {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ because $B_i \subseteq A_{ \pi(i) }$,
so $A_{ \pi(i) } \nsubseteq {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \cap A$ and hence $\pi(i) \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}(A,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \cap A)$.
This shows that $\pi \big( {\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}(B,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \cap X \big) \subseteq {\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}(A,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \cap A)$.
In view of \eqref{87654efg172193p01d2rbtfvcxvoo39}, and since ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}(B)$ is arbitrary, this gives
\begin{equation} \label {8237ter7672893eufhf9}
\pi \big( \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}(B,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \cap X \big) \subseteq \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}(A,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \cap A)  \quad \text{for every ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}(B)$.}
\end{equation}
Keeping in mind that $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B) \neq \varnothing$, we obtain
\begin{align}  \label {uhgu561378e90dewjdbv2aX0}
Y &= \pi( H + \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) ) = \pi( \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) )
= \pi\bigg( {\textstyle \bigcap_{ {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B)} \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}(B,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \bigg)} \\
\notag &= \pi\bigg( {\textstyle \bigcap_{ {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B)}  \big( \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}(B,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \cap X \big) \bigg)} \\
\notag &\subseteq {\textstyle \bigcap_{ {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B)} \pi\big( \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}(B,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \cap X \big)}
\subseteq {\textstyle \bigcap_{ {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B)}  \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}(A,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \cap A) } ,
\end{align}
where the last inclusion follows from \eqref{8237ter7672893eufhf9}.
Since ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \mapsto {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \cap A$ is a surjective map from $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B)$ to $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(A)$, we have
$$
{\textstyle \bigcap_{ {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(B)} \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}(A,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \cap A) } 
= {\textstyle \bigcap_{ {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{q}}} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}}^1(A)} \overline{\ensuremath{\mathbb{M}}}(A,{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{q}}}) } = \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(A) ,
$$
so $Y \subseteq \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(A)$ by \eqref{uhgu561378e90dewjdbv2aX0}.
We have $\operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(A) \subseteq \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(A) \subseteq Y$ by definition, so we obtain $\operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(A)=\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(A)$, i.e., $A$ is saturated in codimension $1$. This proves (a).

(b) Suppose that $H \in \mathscr{X}(B)$. We have $H + \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) \supseteq H \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B)$, so $H + \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B)$.
Since $	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}(B^{(H)}) \neq \{0\}$ (because $H \in \mathscr{X}(B)$) and $\big( B^{(H)} , B^{( H + \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) )} \big) \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm EXT}}$ (by (a)),
Lemma \ref{piud29hdbfdu74heqoir923ft7fbc1oeyt} implies that $	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}( B^{( H + \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) )} ) \neq \{0\}$, so $H + \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) \in \mathscr{X}(B)$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
Let $B$ be a noetherian normal $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$-domain graded by a finitely generated abelian group $G$.
If $B$ is saturated in codimension $1$ then the following hold.
\begin{enumerata}

\item $(B^{(H)},B) \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm EXT}}$ for every $H \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B)$.

\item If $\mathscr{X}(B) \neq \varnothing$ then  $G \in \mathscr{X}(B)$ and $	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}(B) \neq \{0\}$.

\end{enumerata}
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
If $H \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B)$ then $B^{( H + \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) )} = B^{( H + \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) )} = B$,
so Thm \ref{o823y48t2309fnb28}(a) implies that $(B^{(H)},B) = \big( B^{(H)} , B^{( H + \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) )} \big) \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm EXT}}$, which proves (a).
If $H \in \mathscr{X}(B)$ then $H + \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) = H + \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) \in \mathscr{X}(B)$ by Thm \ref{o823y48t2309fnb28}(b), so $	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}(B^{(H + \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B))}) \neq \{0\}$;
since $B^{(H + \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B))} = B = B^{(G)}$, we get  $	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}(B) \neq \{0\}$ and $G \in \mathscr{X}(B)$, proving (b).
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label {987654esdfghjdj4edoodji2d0we9iu9w12twf5}
Let ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and $B$ an affine ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-domain graded over ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ by a finitely generated abelian group $G$.
\begin{enumerata}

\item $\mathscr{X}(B) = \bigcup_{ H \in \mathscr{M}(B) } \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}_H(B)$

\item If $B$ is normal then each element $H$ of $\mathscr{M}(B)$ satisfies $H \supseteq \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)$.

\end{enumerata}
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Let us abbreviate $\mathscr{X}(B)$ and $\mathscr{M}(B)$ to $\mathscr{X}$ and $\mathscr{M}$ respectively.
We may assume that $\mathscr{X} \neq \varnothing$, otherwise the claim holds trivially.

(a) By Cor.\ \ref{8A273gLbv9ncxcavcbo3w982376re5}, we have  $\ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}_H(B) \subseteq \mathscr{X}$ for each $H \in \mathscr{X}$.
Thus, $\mathscr{X} = \bigcup_{ H \in \mathscr{X} } \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}_H(B) $.
Since $G$ is finitely generated,
the poset $( \mathscr{X} , \subseteq )$ satisfies the ascending chain condition.
This implies that for each $H_1 \in \mathscr{X}$, there exists $H_2 \in \mathscr{M}$ such that $H_1 \subseteq H_2$ and hence $\ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}_{H_1}(B) \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}_{H_2}(B)$.
Thus, $\mathscr{X} = \bigcup_{ H \in \mathscr{X} } \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}_H(B) = \bigcup_{ H \in \mathscr{M} } \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}_H(B)$, which proves (a).


(b) Assume that $B$ is normal and consider $H \in \mathscr{M}$.  Then $H + \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) \in \mathscr{X}$ by Thm \ref{o823y48t2309fnb28}(b).
So we have $\mathscr{M} \ni H \subseteq H + \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) \in \mathscr{X}$, which implies $H=H + \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)$ and hence $H \supseteq \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)$.
This proves (b).
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label {87654edfgyudi30piwnf3bwvf2tyweuiklc9Bmo3vA34b6getw63ye}
Let ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and $B$ a normal affine ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-domain graded over ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ by a finitely generated abelian group $G$.
If $B$ is saturated in codimension $1$ then $\mathscr{X}(B) = \varnothing$ or $\mathscr{X}(B) = \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B)$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Suppose that $\mathscr{X}(B) \neq \varnothing$.
Then $\mathscr{M}(B) \neq \varnothing$ by Thm \ref{987654esdfghjdj4edoodji2d0we9iu9w12twf5}(a).
Consider $H \in \mathscr{M}(B)$.
We have $H \supseteq \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)$ by Thm \ref{987654esdfghjdj4edoodji2d0we9iu9w12twf5}(b),
and  $\operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) = \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)$ because $B$ is saturated in codimension $1$,
so $H \supseteq \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)$ and consequently $B^{(H)} = B$.
Since $H \in \mathscr{X}(B)$ we have $	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}( B^{(H)} ) \neq \{0\}$ and hence $	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}(B) \neq \{0\}$.
It then follows from Thm \ref{8237e9d1983hdjyev93} that $	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}( B^{(H')} ) \neq \{0\}$ for all $H' \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B)$,
i.e., $\mathscr{X}(B) = \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B)$.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The conclusion ``$\mathscr{X}(B) = \varnothing$ or $\mathscr{X}(B) = \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B)$'' of Cor.\ \ref{87654edfgyudi30piwnf3bwvf2tyweuiklc9Bmo3vA34b6getw63ye}
means that all rings $B^{(H)}$ with $H \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B)$ have the same graded-rigidity status,
i.e., if one of them is graded-rigid then all of them are (see Def.\ \ref{8hnvnBbslijvxbgxsab8AbN7p03msS726rfXC}).
If we furthermore assume that $G$ is torsion-free then (by Lemma \ref{876543wsdfgxhnm290cAo}) all those rings also have the same rigidity status.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- notation-5: body_md -->
If $B = \bigoplus_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} B_i$ is a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded ring and $d$ is a positive integer then
we define $B^{(d)} = \bigoplus_{i \in d\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} B_i$.  (In other words, $B^{(d)} = B^{(H)}$ with $H = d\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$.)
This is called the {\it $d$-th Veronese subring\/} of $B$.
<!-- end notation-5 -->
<!-- bigremark-10: body_md -->
\label {So87gfXtkdfLO982678wgdyfcfu4ygf654W09}
We will make tacit use of the following facts.
\begin{enumerata}

\item \it If ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ is a field and $B$ is a ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-domain, then every $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-grading of $B$ is over ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$.

\item \it If $B$ is a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded ring then $\ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B) = \big\{\, d\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \, \mid \, d \ge 1 \, \big\}$ if the grading is non-trivial, 
and $\ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B) = \big\{\, d\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \, \mid \, d \ge 0 \, \big\}$ if the grading is trivial.
Consequently, $\big\{\, B^{(H)} \, \mid \, H \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B) \, \big\} = \big\{\, B^{(d)} \, \mid \, d\ge1 \, \big\}$ in both cases.

\end{enumerata}
Part (a) follows from Rem.\ \ref{ijn3eoocnnqppieudbc}.
In part (b), note that if the grading is trivial then $\big\{\, B^{(H)} \, \mid \, H \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B) \, \big\} = \{B\} = \big\{\, B^{(d)} \, \mid \, d\ge1 \, \big\}$.
<!-- end bigremark-10 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label {z0zoxjf5wehghwhedcgcn26sbcdtzezp8q0}
Let ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ be a field of characteristic $0$, let $B$ be a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded affine ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-domain,
and let $d$ be a positive integer.
\begin{enumerata}

\item For each $A \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm KHLND}}(B)$, we have $A^{(d)} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm KHLND}}(B^{(d)})$.

\item The map $	\operatorname{\text{\rm KHLND}}(B) \to 	\operatorname{\text{\rm KHLND}}(B^{(d)})$, $A \mapsto A^{(d)}$, is injective.

\item If $B$ is non-rigid then $B^{(d)}$ is non-rigid.

\end{enumerata}
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- notation-6: body_md -->
\label {5Q43wsdbxhj3403o2iuwyetrd567b8niVuk54hwsert2hj3k}
Let $B = \bigoplus_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} B_i$ be a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded domain.
\begin{enumerate}

\item We define $e(B) = \gcd\big\{\, n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \, \mid \, B_n \neq 0 \, \big\}$.
The number $e(B)$ is called the {\it saturation index\/} of $B$.

\item Let $Z$ temporarily denote the set of all height $1$ homogeneous prime ideals of $B$.
We define $\bar e(B) = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}\big\{\, e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \, \mid \, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z \, \big\}$ if $Z \neq \varnothing$, and $\bar e(B) = e(B)$ if $Z = \varnothing$.
We call $\bar e(B)$ the {\it codimension $1$ saturation index\/} of $B$.

\end{enumerate}
<!-- end notation-6 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label {u6543wsxcvnj28c9w5i746bey} 
The ring $B = \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}[U,V,X,Y] / (UY-VX)$ is a normal domain, and is $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-graded by declaring that $U,V,X,Y$ are homogeneous of degrees $0,0,1,1$.
Clearly, $e(B)=1$. 
Define $Z$ as in Notation \ref{5Q43wsdbxhj3403o2iuwyetrd567b8niVuk54hwsert2hj3k}.
The prime ideal $B_+ = \bigoplus_{ i > 0 } B_i$ belongs to $Z$ and $e( B/B_+ ) = 0$,
so $0 \in \big\{\, e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \, \mid \, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z \, \big\}$ and hence $\bar e(B)=0$.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- bigremark-11: body_md -->
\label {78rc12e2536w7894mcnfbsgnshfr}
Let $B = \bigoplus_{ i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} } B_i$ be a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded domain,
and let $Z$ denote the set of all height $1$ homogeneous prime ideals of $B$.
\begin{enumerate}

\item We have $e(B) \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ and $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) = e(B)\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$.
Moreover, $e(B)=0$ if and only if the grading is trivial.

\item We have $\bar e(B) \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ and $e(B) \mid \bar e(B)$. Moreover, $\bar e(B)=0$ if and only if one of the following holds:
\begin{itemize}

\item $e(B)=0$;

\item $e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) = 0$ for some ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z$;

\item the set $\big\{\, e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \, \mid \, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z \, \big\}$ is infinite.

\end{itemize}

\item {\it If $B$ is noetherian then $\big\{\, e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \, \mid \, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z \, \big\}$ is a finite set.}
Indeed, Prop.\ \ref{89fDCN584uKHJu7u59034uf} and Rem.\ \ref{iutr3nic34ri34765io21p} imply that $\big\{\, \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \, \mid \, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z \, \big\}$ is a finite set.
By part (1) we have $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) = e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$ for all ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z$, so $\big\{\, e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \, \mid \, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z \, \big\}$ is finite.

\end{enumerate}
<!-- end bigremark-11 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label {983bvkslwlia293tfg62zgbnm3kry}
Let $B$ be a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded domain.
\begin{enumerata}

\item $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) = e(B)\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$ and $\operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) = \bar e(B)\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$.

\item $B$ is saturated in codimension $1$ if and only if $\bar e(B) = e(B)$.

\end{enumerata}
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
We already noted that $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) = e(B)\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$.
Let $Z$ denote the set of all height $1$ homogeneous prime ideals of $B$.
If $Z = \varnothing$ then Prop.\ \ref{o98hfng54ye9c72ye6fv11vbdi38} gives $\operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)=\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)$ and the definition of $\bar e(B)$ gives $\bar e(B) = e(B)$,
so $\bar e(B) \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} = e(B) \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} = \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) = \operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B)$, which proves (a) in the case $Z = \varnothing$.
If $Z \neq \varnothing$ then we claim that the following equalities hold:
$$
\operatorname{\bar\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}(B) 
= \bigcap_{ {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z } \operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}( B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} )
= \bigcap_{ {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z } \bigg( e( B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} ) \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \bigg)
= 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}} \big\{\, e( B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} ) \, \mid \, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z \, \big\} \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}
= \bar e(B)\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \, .
$$
Indeed, the first equality is Prop.\ \ref{o98hfng54ye9c72ye6fv11vbdi38},
the second one follows from the fact that $\operatorname{\ensuremath{\mathbb{G}}}( B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} ) = e( B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} ) \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$ for each ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z$,
the third one is the definition of ``lcm'' and the last one is the definition of $\bar e(B)$.
This proves (a).  Assertion (b) follows from (a) and Def.\ \ref{oi8y81726et73e8f0i349rtfyh-sat}.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- bigremark-12: body_md -->
\label {i765edcvbnmkiuyghytrew234tyuiojbvcxsertgbnjuh}
In \cite{Chitayat-Daigle:cylindrical}, saturation in codimension $1$ is only defined for $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded domains,
and the definition is as in part (b) of Lemma \ref{983bvkslwlia293tfg62zgbnm3kry}.
So our notion of saturation in codimension $1$ (Def.\ \ref{oi8y81726et73e8f0i349rtfyh-sat}) generalizes that of \cite{Chitayat-Daigle:cylindrical}.
<!-- end bigremark-12 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label {mMpPiq13096gxvbw5resip0tfs}
Let $B$ be a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded domain and let $d \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\{0\}$.
\begin{enumerata}

\item $e( B^{(d)} ) = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}( e(B), d )$

\item If $B$ is noetherian and normal then $\bar e( B^{(d)} ) = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}( \bar e(B), d )$.

\end{enumerata}
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Follows from Lemmas \ref{GOfBH}, \ref{GandGbarOfBH} and \ref{983bvkslwlia293tfg62zgbnm3kry}.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label {65rfgs01oqksmnxcuyf5g42qywsvnf8}
Let $B$ be a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded domain of characteristic $0$.
\begin{enumerata}

\item For each $D \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}(B) \setminus \{0\}$, there exists a height $1$ homogeneous prime ideal ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ of $B$ satisfying:
\begin{enumerata}
\item some homogeneous element $t \in {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ satisfies $D(t) \neq 0$ and $D^2(t)=0$;
\item  $e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) = e(\ker D)$.
\end{enumerata}

\item $e(B) \mid e( \ker D ) \mid \bar e(B)$ \ \  for all $D \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}(B)$.

\item If $B$ is saturated in codimension $1$ then $e( \ker D ) = e(B)$ for all $D \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}(B)$.

\end{enumerata}
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Follows from Thm \ref{3498huv8oe98y3876wgebf09} and Lemma \ref{983bvkslwlia293tfg62zgbnm3kry}.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- notation-7: body_md -->
\label {NOTA8h7gt23er5w67xxde4c2t3gb9jrdhfgbs8u}
Given a prime number $p$ and any $m \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \setminus \{0\}$, we set 
$$
v_p(m) = \max\big\{\, i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} \, \mid \, \text{$p^i$ divides $m$} \, \big\}.
$$
We also define $v_p(0) = \infty$, so $v_p(0) > v_p(m)$ for all $m \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\setminus\{0\}$.

Given $m \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} \setminus \{0\}$ and $n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$, we define the element $m \odiv n$ of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} \setminus \{0\}$ by 
$$
\textstyle m \odiv n = \prod\limits_{p \in P(m,n)} p^{ v_p(m) }
$$
where $P(m,n)$ is the set of prime numbers $p$ such that $v_p(m) > v_p(n)$.
<!-- end notation-7 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label {8h7gt23er5w67xxde4c2t3gb9jrdhfgbs8u}
The operation $\odiv$ has the following properties.
\begin{enumerata}

\item If $m \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\{0\}$ then $m \odiv 1 = m$ and $m \odiv 0 = 1$.

\item If $m \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\{0\}$ and $n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ then
\begin{itemize}

\item $m \odiv n = 1 \Leftrightarrow m \mid n$,

\item $(m \odiv n) \mid m \mid 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}(m \odiv n , n)$.

\end{itemize}

\item If $B$ is a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded domain then $B^{(m \odiv e(B))} = B^{(m)}$ for all $m \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\{0\}$.

\end{enumerata}
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Assertions (a) and (b) are easy.  We prove (c).
We have  $(m \odiv e(B)) \mid m$ by (b), so $B^{(m \odiv e(B))} \supseteq B^{(m)}$.
To prove the reverse inclusion, consider $x \in  B^{(m \odiv e(B))} \setminus \{0\}$ homogeneous of degree $d$.
Then $0 \neq B_d \subseteq B^{(m \odiv e(B))}$,
so $d$ is a multiple of both $m \odiv e(B)$ and $e(B)$, i.e., $	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}( m \odiv e(B) , e(B) ) \mid d$. 
Since $m \mid 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}( m \odiv e(B) , e(B) )$ by (b), we get $m \mid d$, so $x \in B^{(m)}$.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label {8y3655431qsxdsf2shccvmmlot405cvxj4u1}
Let $B$ be a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded noetherian normal $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$-domain.
Let $d \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\{0\}$ and define $d' = \gcd(d,\bar e(B))$ and $d'' = d' \odiv e(B)$.
Then 
$$
\big( B^{(d)} , B^{(d')} \big) \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm EXT}} \quad \text{and} \quad \big( B^{(d)} , B^{(d'')} \big) \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm EXT}} .
$$
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
We have $\big( B^{(d)} , B^{(d')} \big) \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm EXT}}$ by Thm \ref{o823y48t2309fnb28} and Lemma \ref{983bvkslwlia293tfg62zgbnm3kry}.
It follows that $\big( B^{(d)} , B^{(d'')} \big) \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm EXT}}$, because  $B^{(d'')} = B^{(d')}$
by Lemma \ref{8h7gt23er5w67xxde4c2t3gb9jrdhfgbs8u}(c).
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- notation-8: body_md -->
\label {98y82990294jend939t9uyf}
For each positive integer $d$, let $\mathscr{I}_d = \{d,2d,3d,\dots\}$.
Let $\preceq$ be the partial order on $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\{0\}$ defined by declaring that 
$d_1 \preceq d_2$ $\Leftrightarrow$ $\mathscr{I}_{d_1} \subseteq \mathscr{I}_{d_2}$ $\Leftrightarrow$ $d_2 \mid d_1$.

If $B$ is a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded domain of characteristic $0$, let
$$
	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B) = \big\{\, d \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\{0\} \, \mid \, \text{$B^{(d)}$ is non-rigid} \, \big\}
$$
and let $M(B)$ be the set of maximal elements of the poset $(	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B),\preceq)$.
Note that 
\begin{equation}  \label {oijn23w9e0cnbv2sxcxzq5at}
\text{$B$ is non-rigid $\iff$ $1 \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ $\iff$ $1 \in M(B)$ $\iff$ $M(B) = \{1\}$.}
\end{equation}
<!-- end notation-8 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label {9876f5d43s09ijknm57ffd}
Let ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and $B$ a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded affine ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-domain.
\begin{enumerata}

\item If the grading of $B$ is nontrivial then
$$
\text{$\mathscr{X}(B) = \big\{\, d\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \, \mid \, d \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B) \, \big\}$ \ \ and \ \ $\mathscr{M}(B) = \big\{\, d\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \, \mid \, d \in M(B) \, \big\}$.}
$$

\item If the grading of $B$ is trivial, the following hold.
\begin{enumerata}

\item If $B$ is non-rigid then $	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B) = \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} \setminus \{0\}$ and $M(B)=\{1\}$.

\item If $B$ is rigid then  $	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B) = \varnothing = M(B)$.

\end{enumerata}


\end{enumerata}
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Assertion (b) is clear. We prove (a).
Since the grading of $B$ is not trivial,
we have $\ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B) = \big\{\, d\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \, \mid \, d \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\{0\} \, \big\}$, and
Rem.\ \ref{6543wscvhyuhoblgmrne4b3vf432wsdfw}(b) gives the first equality in:
\begin{align*}
\mathscr{X}(B) &= \big\{\, H \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B) \, \mid \, \text{$B^{(H)}$ is non-rigid} \, \big\} \\
&= \big\{\, d\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \, \mid \, \text{$d \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus \{0\}$ and $B^{(d)}$ is non-rigid} \, \big\} = \big\{\, d\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \, \mid \, d \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B) \, \big\} .
\end{align*}
It follows that $\mathscr{M}(B) = \big\{\, d\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \, \mid \, d \in M(B) \, \big\}$, as desired.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label {p98qy386e523brxhbfc6ghvc63x2345618q30}
Let ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and $B$ a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded affine ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-domain.
\begin{enumerata}

\item $	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B) = \bigcup_{ d \in M(B) } \mathscr{I}_d$


\item If $B$ is normal then each element $d$ of $M(B)$ satisfies
$$
d \mid \bar e(B) \quad \text{and} \quad d \odiv e(B) = d .
$$

\end{enumerata}
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
If the grading of $B$ is trivial then the result easily follows from Lemma \ref{9876f5d43s09ijknm57ffd}(b).
Assume that the grading is nontrivial.
We have $\mathscr{X}(B) = \big\{\, d\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \, \mid \, d \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B) \, \big\}$ and $\mathscr{M}(B) = \big\{\, d\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \, \mid \, d \in M(B) \, \big\}$ by Lemma \ref{9876f5d43s09ijknm57ffd}(a),
so Thm \ref{987654esdfghjdj4edoodji2d0we9iu9w12twf5} and Lemma \ref{983bvkslwlia293tfg62zgbnm3kry} imply that (a) and (b$'$) are true, where 
\begin{enumerata}
\item[(b$'$)] If $B$ is normal then each element $d$ of $M(B)$ satisfies $d \mid \bar e(B)$.
\end{enumerata}
It remains to check that each $d \in M(B)$ satisfies $d \odiv e(B) = d$ (we don't need to assume that $B$ is normal for this part).
Let $d \in M(B)$ and define $d' = d \odiv e(B)$.
We have $B^{(d)} = B^{(d')}$ by Lemma \ref{8h7gt23er5w67xxde4c2t3gb9jrdhfgbs8u}(c), so clearly $d' \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$.
Lemma \ref{8h7gt23er5w67xxde4c2t3gb9jrdhfgbs8u}(b) gives $d' \mid d$, so $d \preceq d'$.
Thus $M(B) \ni d \preceq d' \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$, so $d'=d$, i.e., $d \odiv e(B) = d$.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- corollary-11: body_md -->
\label {1D0x2mv4yhhtfukCs1unc3t46bisgf9f2}
Let ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and $B$ a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded normal affine ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-domain.
If $B$ is saturated in codimension $1$ then $	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B) = \varnothing$ or $	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B) = \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} \setminus \{0\}$.
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Cor.\ \ref{87654edfgyudi30piwnf3bwvf2tyweuiklc9Bmo3vA34b6getw63ye} implies that $\mathscr{X}(B) =\varnothing$ or $\mathscr{X}(B)=\ensuremath{\mathbb{T}}(B)$,
so the claim follows from Lemma \ref{9876f5d43s09ijknm57ffd}.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- corollary-12: body_md -->
\label {o87r62390cJj99xjhs263bfe}
Let ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and $B$ a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded normal affine ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-domain.
\begin{enumerata}

\item For every $d \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\{0\}$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerati}

\item $d \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$

\item $\mathscr{I}_d \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$

\item $\gcd(d,\bar e(B)) \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$

\item $d \odiv e(B) \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$.

\end{enumerati}

\item If $\bar e(B) \neq 0$ and $	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B) \neq \varnothing$ then $\bar e(B) \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$.

\end{enumerata}
<!-- end corollary-12 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
To prove (a), consider $d \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\{0\}$.

If $d \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ then Cor.\ \ref{p98qy386e523brxhbfc6ghvc63x2345618q30} implies that $d \in \mathscr{I}_{m} \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ for some $m \in M(B)$.
Then $\mathscr{I}_d \subseteq \mathscr{I}_{m} \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$, so (i) implies (ii). The converse is obvious, so (i) $\Leftrightarrow$ (ii).

If $d \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ then Cor.\ \ref{p98qy386e523brxhbfc6ghvc63x2345618q30} implies that $d \in \mathscr{I}_{m} \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ for some $m \in M(B)$,
and moreover $m \mid \bar e(B)$. So $m \mid \gcd(d, \bar e(B))$, so $\gcd(d, \bar e(B)) \in \mathscr{I}_{m} \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$
and hence $\gcd(d,\bar e(B)) \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$.
Conversely, if $\gcd(d,\bar e(B)) \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ then  define $d' = \gcd(d,\bar e(B))$ and note that $d \in \mathscr{I}_{d'} \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$
(using that (i) implies (ii)), so $d \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$. So  (i) $\Leftrightarrow$ (iii).

Since $B^{(d)} = B^{( d \odiv e(B) )}$ by Lemma \ref{8h7gt23er5w67xxde4c2t3gb9jrdhfgbs8u}(c),
it is clear that (i) $\Leftrightarrow$ (iv).
This proves (a).

To prove (b), suppose that $\bar e(B) \neq 0$ and $	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B) \neq \varnothing$.
Pick $d \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$; then $\bar e(B) d \in \mathscr{I}_d \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ by (a),
so $\gcd( \bar e(B) d, \bar e(B) ) \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ again by (a), so $\bar e(B) \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label {87t6yfjcbbvo39f8y7-2}
Let ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ be a field and $B = \bigoplus_{ i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} } B_i$ a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded affine ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-domain such that $B_j\neq0$ for some $j>0$.
\begin{enumerata}

\item $\bar e(B) = 0$ if and only if 
$B$ is $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-graded and the prime ideal $B_+ = \bigoplus_{ i > 0 } B_i$ has height $1$.

\item If $B$ is normal and $\bar e(B)=0$, then there exist $s \in B_0 \setminus \{0\}$ and a homogeneous element $t \in B \setminus\{0\}$ of
positive degree such that $B_s = (B_0)_s[t] = \big( (B_0)_s \big)^{[1]}$.

\end{enumerata}
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Before proving (a) or (b), we first note that
\begin{equation} \label {B09F3065-A83D-47C3-9B8B-98259E3CA797}
\text{${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} \subseteq B_0$ and $B_0$ is ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-affine.}
\end{equation}
Indeed, Rem.\ \ref{ijn3eoocnnqppieudbc} gives the first part of \eqref{B09F3065-A83D-47C3-9B8B-98259E3CA797}
and Cor.\ \ref{8Qp98781hy2uexihvcx2qw2wUxq3ew0pokjmnbvaw2345} with $H=0$ gives the second.


Proof of (a). Let $Z$ denote the set of all height $1$ homogeneous prime ideals of $B$.

If $B$ is $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-graded and $	\operatorname{\text{\rm ht}}(B_+) = 1$ then $B_+ \in Z$ and $e( B/B_+ ) = 0$, so $\bar e(B) = 0$
by part (2) of Rem.\ \ref{78rc12e2536w7894mcnfbsgnshfr}.

Conversely, assume that $\bar e(B) = 0$.
Since $\bar e(B) \neq e(B)$, we have $Z \neq \varnothing$;
since $B$ is noetherian, $\big\{\, e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \, \mid \, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z \, \big\}$ is a finite set by part (3) of Rem.\ \ref{78rc12e2536w7894mcnfbsgnshfr};
since $	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}\big\{\, e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \, \mid \, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z \, \big\} = \bar e(B) = 0$, 
there exists ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z$ such that $e( B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} ) = 0$.
Thus,
\begin{equation}  \label {3769ivbx910A28yt}
\text{$B_\ell \subseteq {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ for all $\ell \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} \setminus \{0\}$.}
\end{equation}
Define ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_0 = {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \cap B_0$.
To prove that $B$ is $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-graded, assume the contrary.
Since $B_j \neq 0$ for some $j>0$, this means that there exist $i,j \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$ such that $i < 0 < j$, $B_i \neq 0$ and $B_j \neq 0$.
Choose $x_i \in B_i \setminus \{0\}$ and $x_j \in B_j \setminus \{0\}$;
since $x_i,x_j \in {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$, we have $x_i^j x_j^{|i|} \in {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_0$, so ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_0 \neq 0$.
Since $x_j$ is transcendental over $B_0$, we have $	\operatorname{\text{\rm trdeg}}_{B_0}(B) > 0$;
since ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_0 \neq 0$ and $B_0$ is ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-affine, we have $	\operatorname{\text{\rm trdeg}}_{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}(B_0/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_0) < 	\operatorname{\text{\rm trdeg}}_{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}(B_0) \le 	\operatorname{\text{\rm trdeg}}_{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}(B) - 1$.
On the other hand, we have $B_0/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_0 \cong B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ by \eqref{3769ivbx910A28yt},
so (using $	\operatorname{\text{\rm ht}}{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}=1$ and $B$ is ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-affine) $	\operatorname{\text{\rm trdeg}}_{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}(B_0/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}_0) = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm trdeg}}_{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm trdeg}}_{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}(B)-1$,
a contradiction.

So $B$ is $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-graded and consequently $B_+ = \bigoplus_{ i > 0 } B_i$ is a prime ideal of $B$.
Since $B_j\neq0$ for some $j>0$, we have $B_+ \neq 0$, so $	\operatorname{\text{\rm ht}}( B_+ ) \ge 1$.
We have $B_+ \subseteq {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ by \eqref{3769ivbx910A28yt}, so $	\operatorname{\text{\rm ht}}( B_+ ) = 1$, which proves (a).

Proof of (b). By (a), $B$ is $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-graded and $	\operatorname{\text{\rm ht}}(B_+) = 1$.
By \eqref{B09F3065-A83D-47C3-9B8B-98259E3CA797}, ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}} \subseteq B_0$ and both $B$ and $B_0$ are ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-affine.
Since  $B/B_+ \cong B_0$ and $	\operatorname{\text{\rm ht}}(B_+)=1$, we have $	\operatorname{\text{\rm trdeg}}_{B_0}(B) = 1$.

We first prove the case where $B_0$ is a field.
Let $S = \bigcup_{ i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} }( B_i \setminus \{0\} )$ and $\EuScript{B} = S^{-1}B$.
Then $\EuScript{B} = \bigoplus_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} \EuScript{B}_i$ where $\EuScript{B}_0$ is a field that contains $B_0$.
By Lemma  \ref{i8765redfvbnki8765rfghytrew123456789iuhv},
there exists a nonzero homogeneous element $t \in \EuScript{B}$ of degree $e(B)$ such that
$\EuScript{B} = \EuScript{B}_0[t^{\pm1}]$ is the ring of Laurent polynomials over $\EuScript{B}_0$.
In particular, $	\operatorname{\text{\rm trdeg}}_{\EuScript{B}_0}(\EuScript{B}) = 1$.
We also have $	\operatorname{\text{\rm trdeg}}_{B_0}(\EuScript{B}) = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm trdeg}}_{B_0}(B) = 1$, so $\EuScript{B}_0 / B_0$ is an algebraic extension of fields.
Since $B$ is normal, it follows that $\EuScript{B}_0 \subseteq B$ and hence that $\EuScript{B}_0 = B_0$.
So $B \subseteq \EuScript{B} = B_0[t^{\pm1}]$. Since $B$ is $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-graded, it follows that $B \subseteq B_0[t]$.
Since $B_0$ is a field, it is clear that some monic polynomial $f(t) \in B_0[t]$ belongs to $B$; so $t$ is integral over $B$; since $B$ is normal and $t \in S^{-1}B$,
we get $t \in B$ and hence $B = B_0[t] = B_0^{[1]}$, as desired.

Now consider the general case.
This time, let $S = B_0 \setminus \{0\}$ and $\EuScript{B} = S^{-1}B = \bigoplus_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}} \EuScript{B}_i$, where $\EuScript{B}_0 = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Frac}} B_0$.
It is easy to see that $\EuScript{B}_+ \cap B = B_+$; by basic properties of localization, it follows that $	\operatorname{\text{\rm ht}}(\EuScript{B}_+) = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm ht}}(B_+)=1$.
Since $\EuScript{B}_0$ is a field and $\EuScript{B}$ is an $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-graded normal affine $\EuScript{B}_0$-domain such that $	\operatorname{\text{\rm ht}}( \EuScript{B}_+ ) = 1$,
the preceding paragraph implies that $\EuScript{B} = \EuScript{B}_0[t] = \EuScript{B}_0^{[1]}$ where $t \in \EuScript{B}$ is homogeneous of degree $e(\EuScript{B}) = e(B)>0$.
Multiplying $t$ by an element of $S = B_0 \setminus \{0\}$, we may arrange that $t \in B$.
Since $B$ is ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-affine, we have $B = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[ f_1(t), \dots, f_n(t) ]$ where $f_i(t) \in \EuScript{B}_0[t]$ for all $i$.
Clearly, there exists $s \in S$ such that all coefficients of $f_1(t), \dots, f_n(t)$ belong to $(B_0)_s$.
Thus, $B_s = (B_0)_s[t] = \big( (B_0)_s \big)^{[1]}$, which proves (b).
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- corollary-13: body_md -->
\label {i8976r53g47c8ru3yd3g23ev5627fu}
Let ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and $B = \bigoplus_{ i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} } B_i$ a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded normal affine ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-domain.
If $e(B) \neq 0 = \bar e(B)$ then there exists $D \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}(B) \setminus \{0\}$ such that $\ker(D) = B_0$.  In particular, $B$ is non-rigid.
<!-- end corollary-13 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
First consider the case where $B_j\neq0$ for some $j>0$.
By Lemma \ref{87t6yfjcbbvo39f8y7-2}(b), there exist $s \in B_0 \setminus \{0\}$ and a homogeneous element $t \in B \setminus\{0\}$ of
positive degree such that $B_s = (B_0)_s[t] = \big( (B_0)_s \big)^{[1]}$.
For each $m \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$, $s^m \frac{d}{d t} : (B_0)_s[t] \to (B_0)_s[t]$ belongs to $	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}(B_s) \setminus \{0\}$.
Since $B$ is ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-affine, we can choose $m$ such that $s^m \frac{d}{d t}$ maps $B$ into itself;
then $D = (s^m \frac{d}{d t})|_B : B \to B$ belongs to $	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}(B) \setminus \{0\}$ and $\ker(D) = B_0$.
This proves the result in this case.

If no $j>0$ is such that $B_j\neq0$, then
let $B^-$ be the ring $B$ with the opposite grading, i.e., $B^- = \bigoplus_{ i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} } B_i^-$ where $B_i^- = B_{-i}$ for each $i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$.
We have $e(B^-) \neq 0 = \bar e(B^-)$, and there exists $j>0$ such that $B_j^- \neq 0$.
By the preceding paragraph, there exists $D \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}(B^-) \setminus \{0\}$ such that $\ker(D) = B_0^-$.
Clearly, the same $D$ satisfies  $D \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm HLND}}(B) \setminus \{0\}$ and $\ker(D) = B_0$.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label {finiteprimitiveset534823i93i}
Let ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ be a field of characteristic $0$
and $B$ a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded normal affine ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$-domain.
\begin{enumerata}

\item $M(B)$ is a finite primitive subset of the set of divisors of $\bar e(B)$.

\item If $e(B)=0$ then  $M(B)$ is either $\varnothing$ or $\{1\}$.

\item If $e(B) \neq 0$ and $\bar e(B)=0$ then $M(B) = \{1\}$.

\end{enumerata}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
(b) If $e(B)=0$ then $B^{(d)} = B$ for all positive integers $d$, so $	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ is either $\varnothing$ or $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\{0\}$
and consequently (b) is true.

(c) If $e(B) \neq 0$ and $\bar e(B)=0$ then
Cor.\ \ref{i8976r53g47c8ru3yd3g23ev5627fu} implies that $B$ is non-rigid, so $1 \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ and hence $M(B) = \{1\}$.

(a) It is obvious that $M(B)$ is a primitive set.
If $\bar e(B) \neq 0$ then  Cor.\ \ref{p98qy386e523brxhbfc6ghvc63x2345618q30}(b) implies that $M(B)$ is included in the set of divisors of $\bar e(B)$,
so (a) is true in this case.
If $\bar e(B)=0$ then (b) and (c) imply that $M(B)$ is either $\varnothing$ or $\{1\}$, so (a) is true in this case as well.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- bigremark-13: body_md -->
\label {7cer78543432qq32cr98}
Let us say that a subset $Y$ of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\{0\}$ is {\it realizable\/}
if there exists a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded normal affine $\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}$-domain $B$ satisfying $M(B) = Y$.
Prop.\ \ref{finiteprimitiveset534823i93i} implies that every realizable set is finite and primitive,
but {\it we don't know if every finite primitive set is realizable.}
For instance, we don't know whether $\{6,10\}$ is realizable.
We will learn more about realizable sets in Section \ref{SEC:PhamBrieskornrings}, by studying Pham-Brieskorn rings.
<!-- end bigremark-13 -->
<!-- notation-9: body_md -->
\label {iu7654wd3fg56hxr39ik}
Given ${\mathbf{a}} = (a_1,\dots,a_n) \in ( \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\{0\} )^{n}$ (where $n\ge3$), we define:
\begin{enumerate}

\item $L = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}(a_1,\dots,a_n)$

\item For each $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$,
$J_i = \{1,\dots,n\} \setminus \{i\}$ and $L_i = \displaystyle 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}\big\{\, a_j \, \mid \, j \in J_i \, \big\}$.

\item $S( {\mathbf{a}} ) = S(a_1,\dots,a_n) = \big\{\, j \, \mid \, 1 \le j \le n \text{ and } L_j \neq L \, \big\}$ 

\item The {\it cotype\/} of ${\mathbf{a}}$ is the cardinality of $S({\mathbf{a}})$.  Note that 
$$
	\operatorname{\text{\rm cotype}}({\mathbf{a}}) = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm cotype}}(a_1,\dots,a_n) \in \{0,1,\dots,n\} . 
$$

\item Let $D$ be the set of positive divisors of $\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{L}{L_i}$ and define a map $f : D \to (\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\{0\})^n$
by declaring that if $d \in D$ then $f(d) = (a_1', \dots, a_n') \in (\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\{0\})^n$ where:
\begin{equation}  \label {6gvhb3ag2n60b6tm9rn83h76b54}
a_i' =  \gcd( a_i, L_i ) \, {\textstyle \left[ \frac{L/L_i}{ \gcd( d, L/L_i) } \right] } , \quad 1 \le i \le n .
\end{equation}
It follows from \eqref{6gvhb3ag2n60b6tm9rn83h76b54} that $a_i = a_i' \gcd(d, L/L_i)$ (and hence $a_i' \mid a_i$) for all $i = 1,\dots,n$.
Consequently, $f(1) = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$.

\end{enumerate}
<!-- end notation-9 -->
<!-- notation-10: body_md -->
\label {8r43qasd321qsxcvgttyhnemkrifv90olkmn}
If ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ is a field of characteristic $0$, $n\ge3$ and $a_1,\dots,a_n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\{0\}$, define
$B_{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}; a_1,\dots,a_n} = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[X_1,\dots,X_n] / ( X_1^{a_1} + \cdots + X_n^{a_n} )$.
This is called a {\it Pham-Brieskorn ring}, and it is well known that
$$
\text{$B_{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}; a_1,\dots,a_n}$ is a normal domain.}
$$
Consider the $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-grading of ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[X_1,\dots,X_n]$ such that (for each $i=1,\dots,n$)
$X_i$ is homogeneous of degree $d_i = L/a_i$, where $L = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}(a_1,\dots,a_n)$;
then  $X_1^{a_1} + \cdots + X_n^{a_n}$ is homogeneous and consequently $B_{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}; a_1,\dots,a_n}$ is $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-graded.
We have $B_{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}; a_1,\dots,a_n} = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, where (for each $i$) $x_i \in B_{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}; a_1,\dots,a_n}$ denotes the canonical image of $X_i$.
Clearly, $x_i \neq 0$ is homogeneous of degree $d_i$, and if $n\ge4$ then $x_i$ is a prime element of $B_{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}; a_1,\dots,a_n}$.
<!-- end notation-10 -->
<!-- nothing--5: body_md -->
\label {ConjPn}
For each $n\ge3$, let $\Gamma_n$ be the set of 
$(a_1,\dots,a_n) \in (\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} \setminus \{0\})^{n}$  such that
$$
\text{$\min(a_1,\dots,a_n)>1$ and at most one $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ satisfies $a_i=2$.}
$$
It is well known and easy to see that
\begin{equation}  \label {7y2ew6t2ewoqpoqbgfccxv27}
\text{\it for every $(a_1,\dots,a_n) \in (\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} \setminus \{0\})^{n} \setminus \Gamma_n$, the ring $B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}};a_1,\dots,a_n}$ is non-rigid.}
\end{equation}
It is conjectured (\cite[1.22]{Cheltsov-Park-Prokhorov-Zaidenberg_2021}, \cite{Kali-Zaid_2000}, \cite{FlennerZaidenberg_RatCurRatSing_2003})
that the following statement $\mathscr{P}(n)$ is true for all $n\ge3$:
\begin{description}
\item[$\mathscr{P}(n)$\,] \it \ \ For every $(a_1,\dots,a_n) \in \Gamma_n$, the ring $B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}};a_1,\dots,a_n}$ is rigid.
\end{description}
It is easy to see that if $B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}};a_1,\dots,a_n}$ is rigid then so is $B_{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}};a_1,\dots,a_n}$ for any field ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ of characteristic $0$.
So $\mathscr{P}(n)$ can also be written as follows:
\begin{description}
\item[$\mathscr{P}(n)$\,] \it \ \ 
\begin{minipage}[t]{115mm}
\it
For every field ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ of characteristic $0$ and every $(a_1,\dots,a_n) \in \Gamma_n$, the ring $B_{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}};a_1,\dots,a_n}$ is rigid.
\end{minipage}
\end{description}
The current status of this conjecture is as follows.
\begin{itemize}

\item $\mathscr{P}(3)$ is true, by Lemma 4 of \cite{Kali-Zaid_2000}.

\item $\mathscr{P}(4)$ is true, by \cite{ChitayatPhDThesis} and \cite{ChitayatDubouloz2025}.
(The PhD thesis \cite{ChitayatPhDThesis} shows, among other things, that if 
$B_{ \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}} ; 2,3,4,12 }$ and $B_{ \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}} ; 2,3,5,30 }$ are rigid then $\mathscr{P}(4)$ is true.
These two rings are shown to be rigid in \cite{ChitayatDubouloz2025}.)

\item For $n>4$, only special cases of $\mathscr{P}(n)$ are known to be true. (See for instance Lemma \ref{4uygrfhejrFDfhgsdTHbfd68827djGD763}.)

\end{itemize}
<!-- end nothing--5 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\label {4uygrfhejrFDfhgsdTHbfd68827djGD763}
Let ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ be a field of characteristic $0$, $n\ge3$ and $(a_1, \dots, a_n) \in \Gamma_n$.
If $	\operatorname{\text{\rm cotype}}(a_1,\dots,a_n)\ge n-2$, then $B_{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}};a_1,\dots,a_n}$ is rigid.
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- notation-11: body_md -->
\label {98if9jvs9d772jfpd0vhf9w93uo0541hf9}
Let $B = \bigoplus_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} B_i$ and $B' = \bigoplus_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}} B_i'$ be $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-graded rings.
\begin{enumerate}

\item We write $B \cong B'$ to indicate that there exists an isomorphism of rings $\varphi : B \to B'$
satisfying $\varphi(B_i) = B_i'$ for all $i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$.

\item We write $B \overset{\text{\tiny$*$}}{\cong} B'$ to indicate that there exists an isomorphism of rings $\varphi : B \to B'$
such that, for every $x \in B$, $x$ is homogeneous in $B$ if and only if $\varphi(x)$ is homogeneous in $B'$
(but the degree of $x$ in $B$ is not necessarily equal to that of $\varphi(x)$ in $B'$).
Note that if $B \overset{\text{\tiny$*$}}{\cong} B'$ then $e(B)$ is not necessarily equal to $e(B')$.
Also note that
$$
\text{if $B \overset{\text{\tiny$*$}}{\cong} B'$ then $B$ and $B'$ have the same rigidity status,}
$$
because whether or not $B$ (or $B'$) is rigid is independent of the grading.

\end{enumerate}
<!-- end notation-11 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
\label {o8y7t626rf53deg23489jru3sgbref6}
Let ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}$ be a field of characteristic $0$, $n\ge3$ and $a_1,\dots,a_n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\{0\}$.
\begin{enumerata}

\item The integers $\frac{L}{L_1}, \dots,\frac{L}{L_n}$ are pairwise relatively prime.

\item $e(B_{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}};a_1,\dots,a_n}) = 1$ and $\bar e(B_{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}};a_1,\dots,a_n}) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{L}{L_i}$.

\item $B_{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}};a_1,\dots,a_n}$ is saturated in codimension $1$ if and only if $	\operatorname{\text{\rm cotype}}(a_1,\dots,a_n)=0$.

\item Let $d$ be a positive divisor of $\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{L}{L_i}$ and consider $f(d) = (a_1',\dots,a_n')$ as in part {\rm (5)} of Notation \ref{iu7654wd3fg56hxr39ik}.
Then $( B_{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}};a_1,\dots,a_n} )^{(d)} \overset{\text{\tiny$*$}}{\cong} B_{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}; a_1', \dots, a_n'}$.

\end{enumerata}
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Let $B = B_{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}};a_1,\dots,a_n}$.
For each $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$, $x_i \neq 0$ is homogeneous of degree $d_i$;
so $e(B) = \gcd(d_1,\dots,d_n) = \gcd( \frac{L}{a_1}, \dots, \frac{L}{a_n} ) = \frac{L}{ 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}(a_1,\dots,a_n) } = 1$.
Define 
$$
\hat d_i = \gcd\big\{\, d_j \, \mid \, j \in J_i \, \big\} \quad \text{for each $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$.}
$$
Then $\hat d_1 = \gcd(d_2,\dots,d_n) \linebreak[3]= \gcd( \frac{L}{a_2}, \dots, \frac{L}{a_n} ) = \frac{L}{ 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}(a_2,\dots,a_n) } = \frac{L}{L_1}$,
and by the same argument we get
$$
\textstyle
\hat d_i = \frac{L}{L_i} \quad \text{for all $i \in \{1,\dots n\}$.}
$$
If $i \neq j$ then $\gcd( L/L_i , L/L_j ) = \gcd(\hat d_i , \hat d_j ) = \gcd(d_1,\dots,d_n) = 1$, which proves (a).

(b)  We already proved that $e(B) = 1$.
If $Z$ denotes the set of height $1$ homogeneous prime ideals of $B$ then:
\begin{itemize}

\item for each $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$, some ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z$ satisfies $x_i \in {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$;
\item for each ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z$, at most one $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ satisfies $x_i \in {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$, 
and if  $x_i \in {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ then $e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) = \gcd\big\{\,d_j\, \mid \,j \in J_i\, \big\} = \hat d_i = L/L_i$.

\end{itemize}
It follows that $\big\{\, e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} ) \, \mid \, {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Z \, \big\} = \{ 1,  \frac{L}{L_1}, \dots, \frac{L}{L_n} \}$,
so $\bar e(B) = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}\big( {\textstyle \frac{L}{L_1}, \dots, \frac{L}{L_n} } \big) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{L}{L_i}$, the last equality by (a). 
This proves (b), and (c) follows from (b).


(d)  Let $d$ be a divisor of $\bar e(B) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{L}{L_i}$.
Define $\alpha_i = \gcd(d,\hat d_i)$ for each $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$.
Let us prove that
\begin{equation}  \label {B09876543wexcvbjk0oijhnmlpAoiuy654321qws}
\text{for every $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$,} \qquad \gcd(d_i,\alpha_i)=1, \quad d \mid d_i \alpha_i  \quad \text{and} \quad  a_i = a_i' \alpha_i.
\end{equation}
Indeed, let $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$.
Since  $\alpha_i \mid \hat d_i$ and $\gcd(d_i,\hat d_i) = \gcd(d_1,\dots,d_n) = 1$, the first part of \eqref{B09876543wexcvbjk0oijhnmlpAoiuy654321qws} is clear.
To prove the second part, we first show that
\begin{equation}  \label {uhiw37ug3674g8239re0idk}
\textstyle \text{for all $j \in \{1,\dots,n\}$,\ \ $\frac{L}{L_j}$ divides $d_i \hat d_i$.}
\end{equation}
To see this, we note that $\frac{ d_i \hat d_i }{(L/L_j)} = \frac{ (L/a_i) (L/L_i) }{(L/L_j)} =  \frac{ L_j L }{a_i L_i} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$
because if $i=j$ then $a_i \mid L$ and $L_i \mid L_j$,
and if $i \neq j$ then $a_i \mid L_j$ and $L_i \mid L$. This proves \eqref{uhiw37ug3674g8239re0idk}.
By (a), (b) and \eqref{uhiw37ug3674g8239re0idk}, it follows that $\bar e(B) = \prod_{j=1}^n \frac{L}{L_j}$ divides $d_i \hat d_i$.
Since $d \mid \bar e(B)$, we obtain $d \mid d_i \hat d_i$, so $d$ divides $\gcd(d_i d, d_i \hat d_i) = d_i \gcd(d,\hat d_i) = d_i \alpha_i$,
which proves the second part of \eqref{B09876543wexcvbjk0oijhnmlpAoiuy654321qws}.
For the third part, note that $a_i' \alpha_i = \gcd( a_i, L_i ) \,  {\textstyle \left[ \frac{L/L_i}{ \gcd( d, L/L_i) } \right] } \, \gcd(d, \hat d_i )$
and $\hat d_i = \frac{L}{L_i}$, so $a_i' \alpha_i = \gcd( a_i, L_i ) (L/L_i)$.
On the other hand, 
$\frac{ a_i L_i }{ \gcd(a_i,L_i) } = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}(a_i,L_i) = L$, so $a_i = \gcd( a_i, L_i ) (L/L_i) = a_i'\alpha_i$,
proving \eqref{B09876543wexcvbjk0oijhnmlpAoiuy654321qws}.


Consider a monomial $m = x_1^{\nu_1} \cdots x_n^{\nu_n}$ ($\nu_1,\dots,\nu_n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$) such that $d$ divides $\deg(m)= d_1 \nu_1 + \cdots + d_n \nu_n$.
If $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ then  $\alpha_i \mid d_i \nu_i$ (because $\alpha_i \mid d \mid \deg(m)$ and $\alpha_i \mid \hat d_i$),
so $\alpha_i \mid \nu_i$ by \eqref{B09876543wexcvbjk0oijhnmlpAoiuy654321qws}. This shows that $m \in  {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[x_1^{ \alpha_1 }, \dots, x_n^{ \alpha_n } ]$
and hence that $B^{(d)} \subseteq {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[x_1^{ \alpha_1 }, \dots, x_n^{ \alpha_n } ]$.
By \eqref{B09876543wexcvbjk0oijhnmlpAoiuy654321qws}, we have $d \mid d_i \alpha_i$ and hence $x_i^{\alpha_i} \in B^{(d)}$ for all $i$,
so $B^{(d)} = {\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[x_1^{ \alpha_1 }, \dots, x_n^{ \alpha_n } ]$.
Observing that $( x_1^{ \alpha_1 } )^{a_1'} + \cdots + (x_n^{ \alpha_n })^{a_n'} = 0$ (again by \eqref{B09876543wexcvbjk0oijhnmlpAoiuy654321qws}),
one easily obtains that ${\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}[x_1^{ \alpha_1 }, \dots, x_n^{ \alpha_n } ] \overset{\text{\tiny$*$}}{\cong} B_{{\ensuremath{\rm \bf k}}; a_1', \dots, a_n'}$.
This proves (d).
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label {eion98h38dhb2d203ojfbdt7}
Let $n\ge3$ and $(a_1,\dots,a_n) \in \Gamma_n$.
Let $f : D \to (\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus\{0\})^n$ be the map determined by $(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ as in Notation \ref{iu7654wd3fg56hxr39ik}.
Assume that one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerati}  
\item $\mathscr{P}(n)$ is true,
\item $B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}};f(d)}$ is rigid for each $d \in D$ such that $f(d) \in \Gamma_n$,
\end{enumerati}
and observe that {\rm (i)} implies {\rm (ii)}.
For each $\nu =1,2$, let $I_\nu$ be the set of all $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ satisfying $\gcd(a_i,L_i) = \nu$.
Then at most one element $i_0 \in I_2$ is such that $a_{i_0}=2$, and 
$$
M( B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}; a_1, \dots, a_n} ) = \begin{cases}
\big\{\, a_i \, \mid \, i \in I_1 \, \big\} \cup \big\{\, \textstyle \frac{a_ia_j}4 \, \mid \, i,j \in I_2 \text{ and } i \neq j\, \big\} & \text{if $i_0$ does not exist,} \\[1.5mm]
\big\{\, a_i \, \mid \, i \in I_1 \, \big\} \cup \big\{\, \textstyle \frac{a_i}2\, \mid \, i \in I_2 \setminus \{i_0\} \, \big\} & \text{if $i_0$ exists.} 
\end{cases}
$$
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
Let $B = B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}; a_1, \dots, a_n}$.
Since (i) or (ii) holds and (i) implies (ii), (ii) holds. 
Cor.\ \ref{p98qy386e523brxhbfc6ghvc63x2345618q30} implies that $M(B) \subseteq D$,
and Lemma \ref{o8y7t626rf53deg23489jru3sgbref6}(d) implies that if $d \in D$ then
$B^{(d)} \overset{\text{\tiny$*$}}{\cong} B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}; f(d)}$ and consequently $B^{(d)}$ and $B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}; f(d)}$ have the same rigidity status.
By (ii) and \eqref{7y2ew6t2ewoqpoqbgfccxv27}, $B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}; f(d)}$ is rigid if and only if $f(d) \in \Gamma_n$, so:
\begin{equation}  \label {9876543erfcnbvc9x87654}
\text{for each $d \in D$, \quad $d \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ if and only if  $f(d) \notin \Gamma_n$.}
\end{equation}
Since  $f(1)=(a_1,\dots,a_n) \in \Gamma_n$, \eqref{9876543erfcnbvc9x87654} implies that $1 \notin 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$, so $1 \notin M(B)$.

Also note that $L = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm lcm}}(a_i,L_i) = a_i L_i / \gcd(a_i,L_i)$ for each $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$, so
\begin{equation}  \label {7236yhwebdcv5172wu}
L/L_i = a_i / \gcd(a_i,L_i) \quad \text{for all $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$.}
\end{equation}
Define the sets
$$
U_1 = \big\{\, a_i \, \mid \, i \in I_1 \, \big\} \quad \text{and} \quad  U_2 = \big\{\, \textstyle \frac{a_ia_j}4 \, \mid \, i,j \in I_2 \text{ and } i \neq j\, \big\} .
$$

Suppose that $i \in I_1$. Then \eqref{7236yhwebdcv5172wu} gives $L/L_i = a_i$,
so $a_i \in D$ and the tuple $f(a_i) = (a_1', \dots, a_n')$ satisfies $a_i'=1$ by \eqref{6gvhb3ag2n60b6tm9rn83h76b54};
so $f(a_i) \notin \Gamma_n$ and hence $a_i \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ by \eqref{9876543erfcnbvc9x87654}. Thus,
\begin{equation}  \label {987432sdxcpo09287h6hxcve}
U_1 \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B) .
\end{equation}



Suppose that $1,2 \in I_2$.
For each $i \in \{1,2\}$ we have $\frac{a_i}2 = \frac L{L_i}$ by \eqref{7236yhwebdcv5172wu}, so $\frac{a_1 a_2}{4} = \frac L{L_1}  \frac L{L_2} \in D$
and, by \eqref{6gvhb3ag2n60b6tm9rn83h76b54}, the tuple $f(\frac{a_1 a_2}{4}) = (a_1', \dots, a_n')$ satisfies $a_1' = 2 = a_2'$.
So $f(\frac{a_1 a_2}{4}) \notin \Gamma_n$ and hence $\frac{a_1 a_2}{4} \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ by \eqref{9876543erfcnbvc9x87654}.
More generally, the same argument shows that
\begin{equation}  \label {ZoiugvXEWXzfvWbYHuyt9nJd8r763bncnAt7}
U_2 \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B) .
\end{equation}

Let $d \in M(B)$; since $M(B) \subseteq D$, $f(d) = (a_1', \dots, a_n')$ is defined and (by \eqref{9876543erfcnbvc9x87654}) does not belong to $\Gamma_n$;
so one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerata}
\item $a_i' = 1$ for some $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$,
\item $a_i' = 2 = a_j'$ for some distinct $i,j \in \{1,\dots,n\}$.
\end{enumerata}

Suppose that (a) holds.
Then \eqref{6gvhb3ag2n60b6tm9rn83h76b54} implies that $\gcd(a_i,L_i)=1$ (so $i \in I_1$ and $a_i \in U_1$)
and $\frac L{L_i} = \gcd( d , \frac L{L_i} )$, so $\frac L{L_i} \mid d$.
We have $\frac L{L_i} = a_i$ by \eqref{7236yhwebdcv5172wu}, so $a_i \mid d$ and hence $d \preceq a_i$.
We have $a_i \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ by \eqref{987432sdxcpo09287h6hxcve} and $d$ is a maximal element of $(	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B),\preceq)$, so $d=a_i \in U_1$.
So if (a) holds then $d \in U_1$.

Suppose that (b) holds; here, we might as well assume that $a_1' = 2 = a_2'$.
Since $a_i' \mid a_i$ for all $i$, we see that $a_1$ and $a_2$ are even.
Since $a_1 \mid L_2$ and $a_2 \mid L_1$, both $L_1,L_2$ are even, so $\gcd(a_i,L_i)$ is even for $i=1,2$.
By \eqref{6gvhb3ag2n60b6tm9rn83h76b54}, we obtain that for each $i =1,2$, $\gcd(a_i,L_i) = 2$  and $\frac L{L_i} = \gcd( d , \frac L{L_i} )$, and hence $\frac L{L_i} \mid d$.
It also follows that $1,2 \in I_2$, so $\frac{a_1 a_2}4 \in U_2$ and $\frac{a_1 a_2}4 \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ by \eqref{ZoiugvXEWXzfvWbYHuyt9nJd8r763bncnAt7}.
Since $\gcd( \frac L{L_1} , \frac L{L_2} ) = 1$ and (by \eqref{7236yhwebdcv5172wu}) $\frac L{L_i} = \frac{a_i}2$ for $i=1,2$,
we have $\frac{a_1 a_2}4 \mid d$ and hence $M(B) \ni d \preceq \frac{a_1 a_2}4 \in 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$, which implies that $d = \frac{a_1 a_2}4 \in U_2$.
So if (b) holds then $d \in U_2$.
This proves the first inclusion in:
$$
M(B) \subseteq U_1 \cup U_2 \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B) 
$$
where the second inclusion follows from \eqref{987432sdxcpo09287h6hxcve} and \eqref{ZoiugvXEWXzfvWbYHuyt9nJd8r763bncnAt7}.
If we set $t_i = a_i$ for $i \in I_1$ and $t_i = \frac{a_i}2$ for $i \in I_2$, then $t_i = \frac{L}{L_i}$ for all $i \in I_1 \cup I_2$, so
\begin{equation} \label {654edvbnmki87654esdcvbnhy543}
\text{the family $\big( t_i \big)_{i \in I_1 \cup I_2}$ is pairwise relatively prime}
\end{equation} 
by Lemma \ref{o8y7t626rf53deg23489jru3sgbref6}(a). 
Clearly,
\begin{equation} \label {bvcde45676543wsxcvbhuy6567ujnbxsw2}
U_1 = \big\{\, t_i \, \mid \, i \in I_1 \, \big\}  \quad \text{and} \quad  U_2 = \big\{\, t_j t_k \, \mid \, j,k \in I_2 \text{ and } j \neq k\, \big\} .
\end{equation}
Also note that $t_i>1$ for all $i \in I_1$, and that for $i \in I_2$ we have $t_i = 1$ $\Leftrightarrow$ $i=i_0$ (where $i_0$ is defined in the statement of the Proposition).

We will now use the following (easily verified) fact: {\it if $M(B) \subseteq P \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$ and $P$ is a primitive set, then $M(B)=P$.}

Assume that $i_0$ does not exist. Then $t_i>1$ for all $i \in I_1\cup I_2$, so \eqref{654edvbnmki87654esdcvbnhy543} and \eqref{bvcde45676543wsxcvbhuy6567ujnbxsw2}
imply that $U_1 \cup U_2$ is primitive. Since $M(B) \subseteq U_1 \cup U_2 \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$, we have $M(B)=U_1 \cup U_2$ in this case, as desired.

Assume that $i_0$ exists. Then $i_0 \in I_2$ and $t_{i_0}=1$.
For each $i \in I_2 \setminus \{i_0\}$ we have $t_i = t_{i_0}t_i \in U_2$; so $W \subseteq U_2 \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$, where we define $W = \big\{\, t_i \, \mid \, i \in I_2 \setminus \{i_0\} \, \big\}$.
Moreover, each element of $U_2 \setminus W$ is a product of two elements of $W$.
This implies that $M(B) \cap (U_2 \setminus W) = \varnothing$, because no element of $M(B)$ has a proper divisor that belongs to $	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$.
So $M(B) \subseteq U_1 \cup W \subseteq 	\operatorname{\text{\rm NR}}(B)$.
Since the elements of $U_1 \cup W$ $ = \big\{\, t_i \, \mid \, i \in I_1 \cup I_2 \setminus \{i_0\} \, \big\}$ are pairwise relatively prime and strictly larger than $1$,
$U_1 \cup W$ is primitive. So $M(B) = U_1 \cup W$, as desired.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- corollary-14: body_md -->
\label {8bcnc4n57xdklidsocmo77456}
Let $m,n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ be such that $n\ge3$ and $0 \le m \le n-2$.
Let $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_n \ge2$ be pairwise relatively prime integers such that $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_m$ are odd.
Let $B = B_{ \ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}; \ell_1, \dots, \ell_m, 2\ell_{m+1}, \dots, 2\ell_n }$.
Then 
$$
M(B) = \{ \ell_1, \dots, \ell_m \} \cup \big\{\, \ell_j \ell_k \, \mid \, m+1 \le j < k \le n \, \big\} .
$$
<!-- end corollary-14 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Write $B = B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}}; a_1, \dots, a_n}$ where $(a_1, \dots, a_n) = (\ell_1, \dots, \ell_m, 2\ell_{m+1}, \dots, 2\ell_n )$.
We have $L = 2 \prod_{i=1}^n \ell_i$ and the following hold for all $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$:
$$
\textstyle
\text{$L/L_i = \ell_i$ \quad and \quad
$\gcd(a_i,L_i) = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if $i \le m$,} \\ 2, & \text{if $i > m$.} \end{cases}$}
$$
We claim that $(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ satisfies assumption (ii) of Thm \ref{eion98h38dhb2d203ojfbdt7}.
Indeed, it is easy to see that if $d \in D$ then $f(d) = (\ell_1', \dots, \ell_m', 2\ell_{m+1}', \dots, 2\ell_n')$
where $\ell_i' \mid \ell_i$ for all $i=1,\dots,n$. It follows that $\ell_1', \dots, \ell_n'$ are pairwise relatively prime.
So, if $f(d) \in \Gamma_n$ then $	\operatorname{\text{\rm cotype}} f(d) \ge n-1$, so $B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}};f(d)}$ is rigid by Lemma \ref{4uygrfhejrFDfhgsdTHbfd68827djGD763}.
Thus, assumption (ii) of Thm \ref{eion98h38dhb2d203ojfbdt7} is satisfied.

In the notation of Thm \ref{eion98h38dhb2d203ojfbdt7}, we have $I_1 = \{1,\dots,m\}$, $I_2 = \{m+1, \dots, n\}$ and $i_0$ does not exist,
so $M(B) = \{ \ell_1, \dots, \ell_m \} \cup \big\{\, \ell_j \ell_k \, \mid \, m+1 \le j < k \le n \, \big\}$ by that result.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- corollary-15: body_md -->
\label {C9B83uhAjh309fvn928Ia}
Let $Y$ be a finite primitive set whose elements are pairwise relatively prime. 
Then there exists a Pham-Brieskorn ring $B = B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}};a_1, \dots, a_n}$ satisfying $M(B) = Y$.
<!-- end corollary-15 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
If $Y = \varnothing$ then let $B = B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}};3,3,3}$.
We have $\bar e(B)=1$ by Lemma \ref{o8y7t626rf53deg23489jru3sgbref6}(b), 
so Cor.\ \ref{p98qy386e523brxhbfc6ghvc63x2345618q30} implies that $M(B)$ is either $\varnothing$ or $\{1\}$.
By $\mathscr{P}(3)$, $B$ is rigid, so  $1 \notin M(B)$ and hence $M(B) = \varnothing = Y$.

If $Y = \{1\}$ then let $B = B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}};1, 1, 1}$.  Since $B$ is non-rigid, $M(B) = \{1\} = Y$.

From now on, assume that $Y$ is neither $\varnothing$ nor $\{1\}$. Let $m = |Y| \ge 1$ and let $a_1, \dots, a_m$ be the 
distinct elements of $Y$. Then $a_1, \dots, a_m$ are pairwise relatively prime and $a_1, \dots, a_m \ge 2$.
Choose an integer $c\ge3$ such that  $a_1, \dots, a_m, c$ are pairwise relatively prime and let $B = B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}};a_1, \dots, a_m, c, c}$.

We claim that $(a_1,\dots,a_m,c,c)$ satisfies assumption (ii) of Thm \ref{eion98h38dhb2d203ojfbdt7}.
Indeed, it is easy to see that if $d \in D$ then $f(d) = (a_1',\dots,a_m',c,c)$ where $a_i' \mid a_i$ for all $i = 1,\dots,m$.
Note that $a_1', \dots, a_m', c$ are pairwise relatively prime.
If $f(d) \in \Gamma_{m+2}$ then $a_i'>1$ for all $i$, so $	\operatorname{\text{\rm cotype}}(a_1', \dots, a_m',c,c) = m$
and $B_{\ensuremath{\mathbb{C}};a_1',\dots,a_m',c,c}$ is rigid by Lemma \ref{4uygrfhejrFDfhgsdTHbfd68827djGD763}.
Thus, assumption (ii) of Thm \ref{eion98h38dhb2d203ojfbdt7} is satisfied.

In the notation of Thm \ref{eion98h38dhb2d203ojfbdt7}, we have $I_1 = \{1, \dots, m\}$ and $I_2 = \varnothing$, so 
$M(B) =\{ a_1, \dots, a_m \} = Y$ by that result.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- notation-12: body_md -->
Let $X$ be an integral scheme that is normal and noetherian.
Then we may consider the group $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Div}}(X)$ of Weil divisors of $X$, and the group $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Div}}_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}(X) = \ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}} \otimes_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}} 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Div}}(X)$ of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$-divisors of $X$.
If $f$ is a nonzero element of the function field $K(X)$ of $X$ then the divisor of $f$ is denoted $	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_X(f)$;
so  $	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_X : K(X)^* \to 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Div}}(X)$ is a group homomorphism.
<!-- end notation-12 -->
<!-- nothing--6: body_md -->
\label {Pkcnbvc9w3eidjojf0q9w}
(This is paragraph 5.4 in \cite{Chitayat-Daigle:cylindrical}, with minor edits.)
Let $B = \bigoplus_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}} B_i$ be an $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$-graded noetherian normal domain such that the prime ideal $B_+ = \bigoplus_{i > 0} B_i$
has height at least $2$.
Let $X = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Spec}} B$ and $Y = 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Proj}} B$, which are noetherian normal integral schemes.
We shall now define an injective $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$-linear map $D \mapsto D^*$ from $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Div}}_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}(Y)$ to $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Div}}_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}(X)$.

Note that the function fields of $X$ and $Y$ satisfy $K(X) \supseteq K(Y)$.
Let $Y^{(1)}$ be the set of homogeneous prime ideals of $B$ of height $1$.
Since $	\operatorname{\text{\rm ht}}(B_+)>1$, each element of $Y^{(1)}$ is a point of $Y$; in fact we have $Y^{(1)} = \big\{\, y \in Y \, \mid \, \dim\EuScript{O}_{Y,y}=1 \, \big\}$.
For each ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Y^{(1)}$, $B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \supset B_{({\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})}$ is an extension of discrete valuation rings; let $e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ denote the ramification index of this extension.
Then $e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}\setminus \{0\}$.
If $v^Y_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} : K(Y)^* \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$ and 
$v^X_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} : K(X)^* \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$ denote the normalized\footnote{The word ``normalized'' means that the maps $v^Y_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ and $v^X_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ are surjective.}
valuations of $B_{({\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})}$ and $B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ respectively,
then $v^X_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} (\xi) = e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} v^Y_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}(\xi)$ for all $\xi \in K(Y)^*$.
Let $C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^Y$ (resp.~$C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^X$) denote the closure of $\{ {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \}$ in $Y$ (resp.\ in $X$).
Then $C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^Y$ (resp.~$C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^X$) is a prime divisor of $Y$ (resp.\ of $X$),
and every prime divisor of $Y$ is a $C^Y_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ for some ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Y^{(1)}$.
We define $( C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^Y )^* = e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} C_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^X$ for each ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Y^{(1)}$,
and extend linearly to  a $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}$-linear map $	\operatorname{\text{\rm Div}}_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}(Y) \to 	\operatorname{\text{\rm Div}}_\ensuremath{\mathbb{Q}}(X)$, $D \mapsto D^*$.
It is not hard to see that the linear map $D \mapsto D^*$ is injective and has the following property:
\begin{equation}
\label {PWSoidbfci27wyd}
\text{\it  $\big( 	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_Y(\xi) \big)^* = 	\operatorname{{\rm div}}_X(\xi)$ for all $\xi \in K(Y)^*$.}
\end{equation}
<!-- end nothing--6 -->
<!-- lemma-30: body_md -->
\label {7267e23ro98ifwhe8hfwjd}
Let the assumptions and notations be as in paragraph \ref{Pkcnbvc9w3eidjojf0q9w}.
Let ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} \in Y^{(1)}$ and consider the ramification index $e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ of $B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ over $B_{({\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})}$.
\begin{enumerata}
\setlength{\itemsep}{1mm}

\item There exists a homogeneous element $g$ of ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ such that ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} = g B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$.

\item For any $g$ as in {\rm(a)} we have $\gcd( \deg(g) , e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) ) = e(B)$.

\item  $\displaystyle e_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} = \frac{  e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) }{ e(B) }$

\end{enumerata}
<!-- end lemma-30 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
(a) As $B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ is a discrete valuation ring and hence a principal ideal domain, there exists $g \in {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ such that ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} = g B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$.
We have to show that $g$ can be chosen to be homogeneous.
Note that $v^X_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}(g) = 1$.
Write $g = \sum_{i \in I} g_i$ where $I$ is a finite subset of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ and $g_i \in B_i \setminus \{0\}$ for all $i \in I$.
Since $g \in {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$, we have $g_i \in {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ and hence $v^X_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}(g_i) \ge 1$ for all $i \in I$.
If $v^X_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}(g_i) > 1$ for all $i \in I$ then $v^X_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}(g) > 1$, which is not the case.
So there exists $i \in I$ such that  $v^X_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}(g_i) = 1$. Then  ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} = g_i B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$, which proves (a).

Before proving (b), we show that
\begin{equation}  \label {ikjhhgcgrd6widcjb9wvcr}
\begin{minipage}{.8\textwidth}
If $x,y \in B \setminus \{0\}$ are homogeneous with $x/y \in B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^*$, then there exist homogeneous
$\alpha, \beta \in B \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ such that $x/y = \alpha/\beta$.
\end{minipage}
\end{equation}
To see this, we first choose $u \in B$ and $v \in B \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ such that $x/y = u/v$.
Write $u = \sum_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}} u_i$ and $v = \sum_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}} v_i$ where $u_i,v_i \in B_i$ for all $i$,
and choose $j \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} $ such that $v_j \in B_j \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$.
Then the equality $x\sum_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}} v_i = y \sum_{i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}} u_i$ implies that $xv_j = y u_i$ for some $i$.
So $x/y = u_i / v_j$. If $u_i \in {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ then $u_i/v_j$ belongs to ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$, contradicting $x/y \in B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^*$.
So $u_i \in B_i \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$, which proves \eqref{ikjhhgcgrd6widcjb9wvcr}.

(b) Let $g$ be a homogeneous element of ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ such that  ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} = g B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$. 
Let $\delta = \gcd( \deg(g), e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}))$.
Pick any $i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ such that $B_i \neq 0$ and pick $h \in B_i \setminus \{0\}$.
For some $\nu \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$, we have $h/g^\nu \in B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^*$;
so \eqref{ikjhhgcgrd6widcjb9wvcr} implies that $h/g^\nu = \alpha/\beta$ for some homogeneous $\alpha,\beta \in B \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$.
Then $\delta \mid e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}) \mid \deg(\gamma)$ for each $\gamma \in \{\alpha,\beta\}$.
We have $\deg(h) - \nu \deg(g) = \deg(\alpha) - \deg(\beta)$, so $\delta$ divides $\deg(h) = i$.
This being true for each $i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ such that $B_i \neq0$, we conclude that $\delta \mid e(B)$.
Clearly, $e(B) \mid \delta$; so (b) is true. 


(c) Let $g$ be as in (a) and (b).
Let $\varepsilon = e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})$ and $d = e(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})/e(B) = \varepsilon/e(B)$.
Since $e(B) \mid \deg(g)$,
$\deg(g^d)$ belongs to $\varepsilon \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$, which is the group generated by $\big\{\, i \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}} \, \mid \, (B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})_i \neq 0 \, \big\}$;
so there exist $i,j \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ such that $(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})_i \neq 0$,  $(B/{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})_j \neq 0$, and $\deg(g^d) = i-j$;
consequently, there exist homogeneous elements $u,v \in B \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ such that $\deg(g^d) = \deg(v) - \deg(u)$.
Then $\xi = g^d u / v $ belongs to the maximal ideal ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{m}}}$ of $B_{({\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})}$.
Let us prove that ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{m}}} = \xi B_{({\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})}$.

Consider an arbitrary nonzero element $\frac xs$ of ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{m}}}$, where $x,s \in B \setminus \{0\}$ are homogeneous of the same degree and $s \notin {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$. 
Define  $k = v^X_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}\big( \frac xs \big)$.
Then $k>0$, because $\frac xs \in {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{m}}} \subseteq {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}} B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$; it follows that $\frac{x}{sg^k} \in B_{\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}^*$,
so \eqref{ikjhhgcgrd6widcjb9wvcr} implies that $\frac{x}{sg^k} = \frac{b_m}{c_\ell}$ for some
$b_m \in B_m \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$ and $c_\ell \in B_\ell \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$.
Since  $c_\ell, b_m \in B \setminus {\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}}$, we have $\ell, m \in \varepsilon\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$.
Since  $\frac xs = g^k \frac{b_m}{c_\ell}$, we have $k \deg(g) + m - \ell = \deg(x) - \deg(s) = 0$;
it follows that $\varepsilon \mid k \deg(g)$, or equivalently, $d \mid k \frac{\deg(g)}{e(B)}$.
Part (b) shows that $d = \frac{\varepsilon}{e(B)}$ is relatively prime to $\frac{\deg(g)}{e(B)}$, so $d \mid k$.
Write $k = k_0 d$ (where $k_0>0$), then 
$$
\frac xs = g^{k_0 d} \, \frac{b_m}{c_\ell} 
= \left(g^{d} \frac uv\right)^{k_0} \frac{v^{k_0}b_m}{u^{k_0}c_\ell} 
= \xi^{k_0} \frac{v^{k_0}b_m}{u^{k_0}c_\ell} 
$$
where $\frac{v^{k_0}b_m}{u^{k_0}c_\ell} \in B_{({\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})}^*$.
Since $k_0>0$, we have $\frac xs \in \xi B_{({\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})}$, which shows that ${\ensuremath{\mathfrak{m}}} = \xi B_{({\ensuremath{\mathfrak{p}}})}$.
